passage:
I sit next to Pema at the design studio, so I saw the whole thing on Thursday.
A video was flying around every group: a bridge collapsing, cars sliding into a river, with the caption "Our Ring Road flyover, just now!!" Three people in our office had already shared it. Someone was crying in the pantry.
Pema didn't share it. She paused it, zoomed in, and said, "Those cars are driving on the left, but look at the signs." Then she dragged a frame into an image search. I watched the results load. The same video, from another country, four years ago.
She checked two local news sites next. Nothing about the flyover. She called the office manager to tell the person in the pantry.
I don't know what she was feeling. She looked calm, maybe a little tired. When I asked, she just said, "If I can't find where it came from, I don't send it."
Rashmi

qa.q: How many people in the office had already shared the video?
qa.a: Three people in the office had already shared it.

qa.q: What might Pema have been thinking when she paused the video?
qa.a: Pema probably doubted the caption because details like the road signs did not fit, although Rashmi admits not knowing exactly what she felt.

qa.q: Which of Pema's steps could anyone copy before sharing?
qa.a: Looking at odd details, searching a frame to find where the video first appeared, and checking whether trusted local news carries the story.

qa.q: How was the person crying in the pantry affected by the fake?
qa.a: That person was frightened by a disaster that had not happened here, and Pema's call to the office manager was a way to calm that fear.

grounding: Rashmi watches Pema check a viral disaster video by searching for its source and trusted outlets, and refuse to share what she cannot verify.

passage:
Monday. A screenshot arrived in Imran's alumni group: a news headline saying his old company was shutting its Chennai office, with a logo that looked right. Shankar had already added, "Told you!!" Imran's thumb hovered over forward to his friends still working there. He stopped. No link, just a picture of a headline.
Wednesday. He searched the exact headline. No news site had it. On the company's own press page, the latest note was about a new Chennai hiring drive. He looked at the screenshot again: the font of the date didn't match the rest.
Friday. The fake had reached forty groups. Shankar messaged him privately. "Did you check that thing? My cousin there was panicking."
"I did. It's not real. There's no source anywhere, and the company says the opposite."
"Should've asked you first."
"Next time just don't send it until someone finds the source."

qa.q: What was the latest note on the company's press page about?
qa.a: The latest note was about a new Chennai hiring drive.

qa.q: What does Imran's hovering thumb on Monday suggest Imran was feeling?
qa.a: His thumb hovered over forward and then he stopped, which shows he doubted a headline that came only as a picture with no link.

qa.q: Which checks did Imran do before deciding the story was fake?
qa.a: He searched the exact headline on news sites, checked the company's own press page, and noticed the date font did not match.

qa.q: How has Shankar's view changed by Friday?
qa.a: Shankar is worried because a cousin at the company panicked, and now wishes Imran had been asked first instead of adding "Told you!!".

grounding: Over a week, Imran looks for the original source of a viral headline, checks trusted outlets and odd details, and does not share it.

passage:
Indu, you asked how I learnt to be so slow with news. Sit.
When I was twenty-five, a junior at the district paper, a photographer friend brought me a picture: a burning bus, a crowd, and a caption saying it happened in our town that morning. The editor was out. The page was going to press at ten.
Something bothered me. The crowd was in sweaters, and it was May. The shop sign behind the bus was in a script nobody here uses.
I phoned the police control room: no bus fire today. I rang our reporter near the bus stand: all quiet. I searched the office's old photo files, and there it was, printed years earlier from another state.
My friend was furious. "You'll miss the scoop, Harish." I said, "If I can't check it, it doesn't go." We printed nothing. The next day two other papers apologised for running it.

qa.q: At what time was the page going to press?
qa.a: The page was going to press at ten.

qa.q: What was young Harish feeling while looking at the photo?
qa.a: Young Harish felt uneasy and doubtful; the sweaters in May and the unfamiliar script on the shop sign bothered Harish.

qa.q: Which choice at the turning point kept the paper from a mistake?
qa.a: Checking with the police control room and the reporter near the bus stand, finding the old print, and refusing to run what could not be checked.

qa.q: How did the photographer friend see Harish's decision?
qa.a: The friend was furious about missing a scoop, seeing the checking as a loss rather than as protection.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how checking the source, noticing odd details and missing context, and refusing to print the unchecked photo prevented a false story.

passage:
The power had been out for six hours when the video reached Nazia's phone, battery at 14 percent. Muddy water poured through gates while a panicked voice shouted, "Dam opening tonight! Leave now!"
Vijay, who ran the lane's flood relief group with Nazia, was already typing. "Send it to all 300 families. Better safe."
"Wait. Two minutes." On one bar of signal she opened the district disaster cell's page. No alert. She checked two news sites. Nothing. She played the video again: the trees behind the gates were bare and dry, not a monsoon scene at all.
"If it's real and we wait, people drown," Vijay said.
"If it's fake and we send it, three hundred families run into the dark on flooded roads." She dialled the disaster cell's helpline. Busy. Again. On the third try a tired officer said the dam was holding and that real alerts come only by official message.
Nazia posted that, and nothing else. Her battery hit 9 percent.

qa.q: What did the voice in the video shout?
qa.a: 'Dam opening tonight! Leave now!'

qa.q: What was Nazia likely feeling while Vijay was typing?
qa.a: Nazia was tense and torn under pressure, yet cautious enough to ask for two minutes before anything went to 300 families.

qa.q: Which checks did Nazia run before posting anything?
qa.a: She opened the district disaster cell's page, checked two news sites, noticed the bare, dry trees in the video, and called the helpline until an officer answered.

qa.q: How did Vijay see the risk of waiting?
qa.a: Vijay feared people might drown if the warning was real and they waited, so sharing at once seemed the safer choice.

grounding: Shows an adult under time pressure checking official sources, trusted news and odd details before sharing, and posting only what was confirmed.

passage:
The clip hit the team group at 9:40 in the Hyderabad office: their company head on stage, saying, "By June, all junior roles will be cut." Twelve seconds, no more.
Mridul spun his chair around. "That's us, man. That's literally us."
Jeevan's stomach lurched too. Rent. His sister's fees. But he said, "Where's the full video?"
He found the town hall recording on the company's own page. Forty minutes long. He dragged to the twenty-second minute and turned the volume up. "Some people are saying that by June, all junior roles will be cut. That is a rumour we want to end today."
Mridul read over his shoulder. "They chopped off the first half."
"And the second." Jeevan checked two business news sites; both reported the head promising no junior layoffs.
He didn't forward the clip. He posted the link with the minute marked, then went to get chai. His hands took a while to stop shaking.

qa.q: How long was the clip that hit the team group?
qa.a: Twelve seconds, no more.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when the clip arrived, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Jeevan felt a lurch of fear about rent and his sister's fees, and his hands took a while to stop shaking even after checking.

qa.q: Which checks did Jeevan use before sharing anything?
qa.a: Finding the full town hall recording on the company's own page, listening at the twenty-second minute, and checking two business news sites; then posting the link, not the clip.

qa.q: What would change if Jeevan had forwarded the clip?
qa.a: Juniors across the office would panic over words that were actually the head denying the rumour.

grounding: Shows an adult finding the original full recording, checking trusted outlets and spotting missing context before sharing anything.

passage:
"Chinmay, look. The flyover near the station collapsed this morning!" Maria pushed her phone across the breakfast table.
"Hang on." He watched it twice. "Where does it say that?"
"The caption. Our city, today, share fast."
"Who posted it first?"
"Some page called City Alerts 24."
"Let's see what the local news sites say." He searched. "Nothing. Not one of them. A flyover falling would be everywhere."
"Maybe it just happened."
"Maybe. But look at the buses. Red double-deckers. Ours are green." He paused the frame. "And the shop signs aren't in any language we read here."
Maria leaned closer. "Okay, that's weird."
He ran an image search on one frame. "Here. Same video, another country, three years ago."
"So it's real, just not here."
"Real clip, wrong story. And if I couldn't find anything either way, I still wouldn't share it."
Maria deleted the forward she'd half-typed to her office group.

qa.q: What colour are the buses in their city?
qa.a: Green.

qa.q: What made Maria stop before forwarding?
qa.a: Maria felt alarmed at first, then puzzled and doubtful once Chinmay pointed out the red double-deckers and the unfamiliar shop signs.

qa.q: Which checks did Chinmay use?
qa.a: He asked who posted it first, searched local news sites, noticed odd details like the buses and signs, and ran an image search on a frame.

qa.q: What would change if Maria had forwarded it to her office group?
qa.a: Colleagues might panic or avoid the station, and a wrong story would spread further under Maria's name.

grounding: Shows an adult tracing a clip's original source, checking trusted outlets and odd details, and not sharing what cannot be checked.
